title: How does traffic policy divide requests among pods?
answer: The load balancer weighs nodes, not pods

checks.question: With pods placed 3, 1, 0 on three nodes and externalTrafficPolicy Local, why does pod d get three times the requests of pod a?
checks.answer: Node 3 runs no pod and fails the health check, so the load balancer gives Node 1 and Node 2 half each. Node 1 splits its half three ways (1/6 per pod); Node 2 gives all of its half to pod d.

checks.question: A node’s iptables chain lists three pods. With what probabilities do its rules match, and what share does each pod get?
checks.answer: 1/3, then 1/2, then always: rule i of n matches with probability 1/(n−i), so each pod gets 1/3 of what the node receives.

checks.question: With pods placed 2, 2, 0, are Local’s shares even?
checks.answer: Yes. Node 1 and Node 2 each get half and each splits it two ways, so every pod gets 1/4: Local is even when every node with pods runs the same number.

steps.title: 4 pods on three nodes behind one load balancer
steps.line: Predict: with externalTrafficPolicy Local, which pod gets the most requests?
steps.caption: A Service of type LoadBalancer: a cloud load balancer sends outside requests to the nodes, and rules that kube-proxy writes on each node hand every request to a pod. Node 1 runs 3 pods, Node 2 runs 1 and Node 3 runs none. The Service’s externalTrafficPolicy sets which pods a node may pick: under Cluster, the default, any pod in the cluster; under Local, only the pods on that node. This one is set to Local.
steps.picture: Architecture diagram: 8 services, 7 edges; 4 labelled values.

steps.title: Under Local, each node’s rules list only its own pods
steps.line: Probabilities 1/(n−i) give each pod 1/3 of the node’s requests.
steps.caption: In iptables mode kube-proxy tries one rule per pod in order. For three candidates, the first takes 1/3 of requests; the second sees the remaining 2/3 and takes half of those, another 1/3 overall; the last gets the remaining 1/3. In general, rule i of n matches 1/(n−i) of the requests that reach it, counting i from zero, so each pod gets 1/n of the node’s traffic. Under Local Node 1 lists only its 3 pods: 1/3, 1/2, always, so each gets 1/3 of what Node 1 receives.
steps.picture: Architecture diagram: 8 services, 7 edges; Code, 4 lines. Note: “1/3” beside Pod a; “1/3” beside Pod b; “1/3” beside Pod c; chain shown: Node 1 · 10.240.0.1. New in this step: Code, 4 lines.

steps.title: Node 3 runs no pod, so it fails the health check
steps.line: Node 1 and Node 2 answer 200 and each get 1/2 of requests.
steps.caption: Under Local, kube-proxy answers the load balancer’s health check on each node: 200 when the node runs a pod of the Service, 503 when it runs none. The load balancer stops sending to Node 3. It divides requests equally among healthy nodes, regardless of their pod counts, so Node 1 and Node 2 each get 1/2 of the requests. The next choice happens inside each node: its share is divided among its own pods.
steps.picture: Architecture diagram: 8 services, 7 edges. Note: “200, 3 local pods” beside Node 1 · 10.240.0.1; “200, 1 local pod” beside Node 2 · 10.240.0.2; “503, 0 local pods” beside Node 3 · 10.240.0.3; fails the health check: Node 3 · 10.240.0.3.

steps.title: Answer: pod d gets 1/2 of the requests; pods a, b and c get 1/6 each
steps.line: Split by node, not pod: each node with pods gets 1/2.
steps.caption: The load balancer weighs nodes, not pods: Node 1 and Node 2 each get 1/2. Node 1 splits its 1/2 three ways; Node 2 sends all of its 1/2 to pod d, so pod d gets 3 times as many requests as pod a.
steps.picture: Architecture diagram: 8 services, 7 edges. Note: “16.7%” beside Pod a; “16.7%” beside Pod b; “16.7%” beside Pod c; and 1 more.

steps.title: With 3, 1, 0 pods, Local trades even load for the client’s address
steps.line: Cluster sends 2 in 3 requests to another node; Local sends none.
steps.caption: Cluster spreads requests evenly over the pods, but 2 in 3 cross to another node and every pod sees a node’s address. Local keeps each request on its node with the client’s address. The load balancer weighs nodes, not pods, so pod d takes 3 times the load of pod a.
steps.picture: Architecture diagram: 8 services, 7 edges; “Cluster”, 3 labelled values; “Local”, 4 labelled values. New in this step: “Cluster”, 3 labelled values; “Local”, 4 labelled values.

steps.title: What these shares leave out
steps.line: Shares are iptables-mode averages; IPVS defaults to round robin.
steps.caption: The shares are long-run averages for kube-proxy’s iptables mode; IPVS mode defaults to round robin. kube-proxy’s health check reports each node’s pod count in a header, but the docs warn that some cloud load balancers cannot weight nodes. Topology-aware routing and session affinity are left out.
steps.picture: Architecture diagram: 8 services, 7 edges; 5 labelled values. New in this step: 5 labelled values.

steps.title: The request stays on its node and keeps the client’s address
steps.line: Pod a sees 198.51.100.79: no source NAT and no second hop.
steps.caption: Node 1’s rules list only its own pods, so the request never leaves Node 1, and kube-proxy adds no source NAT for it. Pod a sees the client’s address, 198.51.100.79. Under Local no outside request takes a second hop.
